content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents an empirical study on the efficacy of representation learning via auxiliary tasks in deep RL. It reviews commonly-used auxiliary tasks in the literature and specifically compares three popular auxiliary tasks, i.e., (1) reward prediction (rwp), (2) forward state prediction (fsp), and (3) forward state difference prediction (fsdp), on their effectiveness for improving RL sample efficiency and asymptotic performance. More specifically, the representations are learned using a decoupled neural network (OFENet) with one of the three auxiliary tasks, and the original RL task is trained with TD3/SAC on a separate network taking learned representations from OFENet as inputs. Different from prior works which mostly studied auxiliary tasks with imagery state inputs, this paper focuses on vectorized state inputs, e.g., measurements captured from a simulated robot, and continuous control problems. The authors experimented on 5 environments with varying complexity, and conclude that learning representations with auxiliary tasks is beneficial for environments of high complexity, and that learning environment dynamics, e.g., fsp or fsdp, is preferable to predicting rewards, e.g., rwp.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Representation learning is an important and interesting topic in deep RL, and learning representations with auxiliary tasks provides a simple yet effective way for extracting useful information from RL observations. So, I believe the paper is relevant to broad research in the RL community. Overall, the paper is well-written and organized, and the related work is adequately cited. 

My main concern is that the paper only presents limited new knowledge and may not bring sufficient value to the community. Major claims, such as “auxiliary task is beneficial for complex environments” and “learning dynamics is more helpful than predicting rewards”, are technically sound, but RL practitioners/researchers are likely to figure these out by intuition even without reading the paper. It is also unclear what are the novel findings on the continuous control problems that are different or unobserved from prior works (e.g., on Atari games). Additionally, I believe the authors could have conducted more in-depth analysis from their experiments to provide more insights to the readers.        


Questions/comments that I believe can improve the overall quality of the paper, if addressed adequately in the revision:

- [Decoupled vs. coupled] It is unclear to me that why decoupled representation learning is preferred over coupled (or implicit) representation learning. I had an impression that representations were mostly learned in a coupled way in earlier works [1][2], e.g., spinning out separate prediction heads for auxiliary tasks while sharing the bottom layers with the main RL task. I would suggest comparing decoupled learning against coupled representation learning (with auxiliary tasks) in the experiments to provide evidence and more insights to the readers on when coupling (or decoupling) should be preferred over the other. 

- [fsp vs. fsdp] Currently, the results and performance of fsp and fsdp are similar in the paper. To better understand the limit of the two and to validate that “fsp is more robust to noise or stark changes between successive observations”, it would be helpful to compare the two auxiliary tasks on some stochastic or noisy environments. Alternatively, the authors may consider manually adding noises to the observations and see how performance would change when the amount of injected noise varies. 

- [fsp/fsdp + rwp] A combination of fsp/fsdp with rwp can be added to the experiments to see if adding rwp can further improve the performance. Although “the combination of several tasks never clearly outperformed the respective best individual tasks” in [2], the representations were learned in a coupled way and the observations in [2] may not generalize to the decoupled settings.   

- [Sample Efficiency] Did you include the pretraining steps in the calculation of sample efficiency? Although the number of pretraining steps can be relatively small, it should be still added as an “offset” in Figures 4, 5, and 6 to establish a fair comparison with the baselines. 

- [FetchSlideDense-v1] It is not clear to me why auxiliary tasks make FetchSlideDense-v1 learnable for TD3 (without HER), but not for SAC. I believe more in-depth analysis is needed to understand what’s the real difference between the two cases. The authors claimed that “the simplification of the learning problem” could be the contributor, but such a simplification is enabled for both TD3 and SAC, right? They also argued that “the learned representation might contain more informative features encoding distance between the arm and the puck”, which I feel can be a valid point, but could you validate this statement in the experiments? It may also help compare the samples collected by TD3 and by SAC, or compare the representations learned with TD3 and SAC, and see/virtualize the difference. Or is it related to exploration strategy used by TD3/SAC? 

- [Pretraining] How data was collected during pretraining? Were actions randomly selected in the pretraining phase?          


Additional comments that do not affect the score/assessment:

- It’s worth discussing some of the disadvantages of using auxiliary tasks for solving RL problems. The authors have mentioned about the increase in the computational time, but is there anything else? Perhaps, non-stationarity? Since the state representations keep evolving during the course of training, learning with auxiliary tasks makes the RL problem non-stationary. More discussion is welcomed in the revision. 

- In Figure 8 and 9 in the appendix, the patterns for TD3 and SAC look very different on some of the environments, e.g., Hopper-v2 and Humanoid-v2. Again, more in-depth discussion and comparison between the two scenarios can be very helpful.    



[1] Jaderberg, Max, et al. "Reinforcement learning with unsupervised auxiliary tasks." arXiv preprint arXiv:1611.05397 (2016).

[2] Shelhamer, Evan, et al. "Loss is its own reward: Self-supervision for reinforcement learning." arXiv preprint arXiv:1612.07307 (2016).

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an empirical comparison of different auxiliary tasks in continuous control benchmark environments. The authors compared three auxiliary tasks, i.e., reward prediction, forward state prediction, and forward state difference predictions, with two baselines algorithms namely TD3 and SAC. These baseline algorithms and their auxiliary-task-augmented variants are evaluated in five continuous control tasks with different complexities. Overall, auxiliary tasks improved the sample efficiency and the final return. Improvements are more significant in more complex environments. The authors further observe that reward prediction is in general less effective than forward state prediction and forward state difference prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strength
* 1. Overall, the paper is easy to follow. The algorithm choices and environment choices are clearly presented. The empirical results are discussed thoroughly.

# Weakness
* 1. The coverage of auxiliary tasks in the empirical comparison is inadequate. Several self-supervised learning auxiliary tasks were proposed for state representation learning in the past years and demonstrated strong performance. Examples include CURL [3], PBL [2], ATC [4], and so on. This paper would be strengthened if these more recent auxiliary tasks are included in the empirical study. It is also worth mentioned that the HER algorithm used in the experiments can be used as a good auxiliary task as well [6]. 
* 2. The choice of the environments are questionable. In 3 out of 5 environments, the tasks are either too easy or too hard that the learning curves are highly overlapped and cannot distinguish different algorithms. A clear distinction is only seen in HalfCheetah and Humanoid. The empirical findings would be more convincing if the auxiliary tasks are evaluated on a wider range of continuous control tasks such as the DeepMind control suite [5].
* 3. One of the main conclusions is that reward prediction is less effective as an auxiliary task than environment dynamic predictions. In Section 3, the authors discussed that reward prediction can only be applied in tasks with non-trivial rewards. However, such a limitation can be partially overcame by a more general form of reward prediction, i.e., multi-horizon value prediction [1]. The conclusion would be more convincing if multi-horizon value prediction is included in the empirical comparison as a stronger version of reward prediction.

# Questions and minor concerns
1. Why is pretraining necessary for the study? Pretraining gives advantages to algorithms with auxiliary tasks in comparison to the baseline algorithms. This choice needs to be justified.
2. Section 5 says that the OFENet and the RL networks are updated alternatively. Could the author clarify what they mean by "alternate"?
3. In the last paragraph of Section 6.1, they authors say "For FetchSlideDense-v1 the representation might for instance contain a feature encoding distance between arm and puck, instead of just the absolute positions from raw observations." This is a rather vague conjecture that is not verified. But there is a simple way to test it: we can train a linear function to predict the distance between the arm and the the puck and see if predicting from the learned representations is more accurate than predicting from the raw observations.

**References**
1. Fedus _et al_ 2019, Hyperbolic Discounting and Learning over Multiple Horizons
2. Guo _et al_ 2020, Bootstrap Latent-Predictive Representations for Multitask Reinforcement Learning
3. Srinivas _et al_ 2020, CURL: Contrastive Unsupervised Representations for Reinforcement Learning
4. Stooke _et al_ 2021, Decoupling Representation Learning from Reinforcement Learning
5. Tassa _et al_ 2019, DeepMind Control Suite
6. Veeriah _et al_ 2018, Many-Goals Reinforcement Learning
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* Clarity: The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
* Quality: The empirical results are clearly presented and thoroughly discussed. But the conclusions are not very convincing due to the weakness mentioned above.
* Novelty: Limited. This paper does not propose any novel technical ideas. As a purely empirical study, the significance of the insights are undermined by the weakness mentioned above.
* Reproducibility: Fair. The authors did not provide the sourcecode for the experiments. But detailed configurations are provided in the appendix.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although clearly written, this empirical paper is limited by the coverage of auxiliary tasks that are evaluated and the environments used for evaluation. The conclusions drawn from the empirical study are questionable and may not be generally applicable. Thus the impact of this paper is limited.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper compares common auxiliary losses used in RL like state and reward prediction heads on a number of tasks with both SAC and TD3 agents. Both agents are augmented with a particular architecture called OFENet for representation learning. The main findings of the paper is that representation learning can provide benefits in learning efficiency on more complex tasks and generally next observation prediction is more useful than reward prediction.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper is generally well written, with many results and a reasonably complete Appendix. However I do not think the central thesis is that useful. It is widely accepted in the community that auxiliary task heads are useful for learning and while the finding that reward prediction is less useful that state based prediction is mildly interesting, I do not think there are enough insights in this work as things stand. 

I think there are questions that are less clear which the authors could focus on and potentially make the paper more interesting. One major one is the use of vision observations - learning robust visual representations that can operate well in the real world is an open problem for which insights would be quite useful. Another question that could be interesting to pursue would be to tease apart the relative importance of represenations in the value function and in the policy. The current setup ties the representations together with the OFENet since the same shared state embediding is sent to both poilcy and value function. But a slight variation of the architecture that could help shed light on how the representation is being used and how to design better representations would be useful and significant.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is clearly written but I do not think any novel insights are provided.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think in its current form the paper is not of sufficient standard for this venue. I encourage the authros to continue working on this though with more weight on understanding where the advantages stem from and how to learn and design better representations for RL especially in visually complex domains.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper presents an empirical comparison of using auxiliary tasks for training representations _explicitly_, which means as a separate task from control learning, on a number of continuous control tasks. The authors argue that this type of representation learning with auxiliary tasks is most beneficial for more complex environments, and that it is best to learn environment dynamics over predicting rewards.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
# Strengths
The paper

# Weaknesses
The main weakness of this paper is that it is too focused on one specific method for learning representations via auxiliary tasks. This makes the findings, while interesting, limited to their particular setting; it is not clear whether the findings would generalize to other training methodologies.

## Algorithms
The RL algorithms considered are only two actor-critic methods. For greater applicability the authors should include at least one value-based method.

## Environments
Only deterministic continuous-control environments are considered. It would be good to also evaluate on discrete control and stochastic environments (Atari with sticky actions would give you both, for instance).

## Architectures
Experiments are only run using OFENet. Although I don't disagree that this could be a reasonable choice for this type of representation learning, it is not clear whether this generalized to other architectures or training scenarios. In particular, a popular way of using auxiliary tasks for representation learning is to use multiple heads from a main network backbone. The results in this paper seem to only apply to the case where representations are learned separately from control, which is not what is most commonly done in the literature.

## Evaluation
In section 5 it says "In all cases, we pretrain OFENet by a certain number of steps". On what data is it pretrained? Is this data made available during the online training phase?

More critically, the authors then say "We set training steps to 0 when pretraining is completed and the RL algorithm starts training." This is not a fair comparison with the baselines, which train on raw observations (so no OFENet), and thus do not benefit from this pre-training phase.

HER seems to play a large role in many of the analyses and conclusions. While HER is an interesting algorithm, it is not the main focus of this paper (nor necessary for representation learning), so it seems to confound some of the results. Further, some of the "findings" around HER seem to be things that have already been known in the literature (as poinoted out by the authors themselves).

Finally, the analyses are quite specific to the few environments considered, so once again it is not clear whether they generalize to other training setups and environments.

## Related literature
There are a number of related works that are not discussed nor mentioned, and which further limit the scope of applicability of this paper:
* [Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Jimmy Ba, Mohammad Norouzi. Dream to Control: Learning Behaviors by Latent Imagination. ICLR 2019.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1912.01603)
* [Danijar Hafner, Timothy Lillicrap, Mohammad Norouzi, Jimmy Ba. Mastering Atari with Discrete World Models. ICLR 2020.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02193)
* [David Ha, Jürgen Schmidhuber. Recurrent World Models Facilitate Policy Evolution. NeurIPS 2018.](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2018/hash/2de5d16682c3c35007e4e92982f1a2ba-Abstract.html)
* [Marc Bellemare, Will Dabney, Robert Dadashi, Adrien Ali Taiga, Pablo Samuel Castro, Nicolas Le Roux, Dale Schuurmans, Tor Lattimore, Clare Lyle. A Geometric Perspective on Optimal Representations for Reinforcement Learning. NeurIPS 2019](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2019/hash/3cf2559725a9fdfa602ec8c887440f32-Abstract.html)
* [Rishabh Agarwal, Marlos C. Machado, Pablo Samuel Castro, Marc G. Bellemare. Contrastive Behavioral Similarity Embeddings for Generalization in Reinforcement Learning. ICLR 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.05265)
* [Amy Zhang, Rowan McAllister, Roberto Calandra, Yarin Gal, Sergey Levine. Learning Invariant Representations for Reinforcement Learning without Reconstruction. ICLR 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.10742)
* [Pablo Samuel Castro, Tyler Kastner, Prakash Panangaden, Mark Rowland. MICo: Improved representations via sampling-based state similarity for Markov decision processes. NeurIPS 2021.](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2021/hash/fd06b8ea02fe5b1c2496fe1700e9d16c-Abstract.html)
* [Lili Chen, Kevin Lu, Aravind Rajeswaran, Kimin Lee, Aditya Grover, Michael Laskin, Pieter Abbeel, Aravind Srinivas, Igor Mordatch. Decision Transformer: Reinforcement Learning via Sequence Modeling.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01345)
* [Han Wang, Erfan Miahi, Martha White, Marlos C. Machado, Zaheer Abbas, Raksha Kumaraswamy, Vincent Liu and Adam White. Investigating the Properties of Neural Network Representations in Reinforcement Learning. IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON PATTERN ANALYSIS AND MACHINE INTELLIGENCE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.15955).

# Suggestions / Questions
1. In section 3 it is not clear whether the authors are considering discounted or undiscounted, and finite or infinite horizon problems. Would be better to specify.
1. In page 3: "**Forward state prediction (fsp)** is the task of predicting $o_{t+1}$..." is this really predicting or generating?
1. In the paragraph about **inverse dynamics models** in page 3 there is the statement "We cannot use the _inv_ task here because...". I don't think this statement is true: you could just use transitions from the replay buffer and not have to get $o_{t+1}$ directly from the environment.
1. One of the conclusions in section 6.2 is that "The _rwp_ task performs worst out of the three...". This is not that surprising, as it's substantially less ibnformation being predicted. This is discussed further down, but I don't think it merits such a prominent place in the discussion.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is well written and easy to follow. The novelty is quite limited, as the findings seem to only apply to the very specific experimental setup the authors considered in this work.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Overall I found the results interesting and somewhat insightful. However, I think the paper is too focused on one specific form of using auxiliary tasks for representation learning and a small set of evaluations (see details above), so it's not at all clear whether the findings generalize to other settings.

I think in its current form it would be a good technical report, but I don't think it's ready for an ICLR publication. To strengthen the work I'd encourage the authors to consider other ways of using auxiliary tasks for representation learning.
